Categories: EDA, yieldWerx

Key takeaways ▼

Osman Chaudry is a business and technology leader with over 25 years of experience in software development, investment management, and e-commerce. With a Bachelor of Engineering (BEng) in Information Systems Engineering from Imperial College London, he has a proven track record of driving success in both global enterprises and startups across Europe, the USA, and Asia. Osman began his career at Goldman Sachs International, where he held multiple leadership roles in the Technology Division. He then led departments at NETSOL, a leading software provider for the asset finance industry. Osman also held several C-level positions at Cheetay, an e-commerce and logistics startup.

What brought you to yieldWerx ?
I’ve spent two decades in the software world, and I joined yieldWerx because we sit at a really exciting intersection: applying modern software agility to the precision of semiconductor manufacturing. Helping our customers maximize yield is a real, high-value problem. My goal is to help our teams execute at their best so we can keep raising the bar for the industry.

What is the biggest challenge your customer is facing?
Honestly, it comes down to the multitude, volume, and variation of data generated across different testers, inline inspection systems, and multiple layers of processing, and the difficulty of making sense of it all. Many customers’ data resides in completely siloed formats, such as STDF, KLARF, parametric logs, and other proprietary files.

Engineers spend a significant amount of time scripting solutions that work for their initial designs. But as systems become more complex and integrated, those patches and scripts become increasingly difficult to maintain and interpret. They need ways to merge data across these sources, investigate why a lot has drifted, identify where manufacturing problems originated, and contain those issues before they affect production further. When you’re trying to move into a complex volume ramp or tighten process control limits, that data friction becomes a significant challenge.

Why is your approach to solving this problem unique?
We take pride in our white-glove deployments. We don’t simply hand over a tool and leave the customer to figure things out. We work directly with each team to resolve their data challenges and map out a long-term data strategy. Rather than forcing teams to immediately replace their existing systems or build massive custom data lakes from scratch, we’ve architected yieldWerx to support both greenfield and brownfield implementation models. We can deploy alongside a customer’s existing infrastructure, allowing data to reside in both repositories and minimizing disruption, or implement a new environment from the ground up. Giving customers these options helps reduce deployment risk. We built yieldWerx as a unified data repository with intelligent data ingestion built in.

We focus heavily on modularity and true end-to-end traceability. Whether an engineer needs automated lot disposition, multidimensional wafer merging, or real-time dynamic PAT (Part Average Testing), the system can be configured around their specific workflows without requiring an army of internal data scientists just to keep dashboards running.

What other approaches are being used to solve this problem?
There are a few different approaches that I see. Some companies build their own infrastructure, using internal scripts and custom analytics to bring together information from different systems. Others rely on individual tools that address specific parts of the process, such as test data analysis, equipment monitoring, or quality management.

These approaches can work well within a defined environment, particularly when the manufacturing process is relatively contained. The challenge comes when you need to connect information across multiple manufacturing stages, test platforms, and ecosystem partners. Maintaining those connections can become a substantial engineering effort.

We’re also seeing greater interest in cloud data platforms and centralized data lakes. These provide useful infrastructure for storing and accessing large amounts of information, but having the data in one place doesn’t necessarily mean it’s organized in a way that manufacturing engineers can use. The data still needs to be interpreted in the context of the process, product, and genealogy. I think the industry is moving toward a more integrated approach, where data infrastructure, manufacturing knowledge, and analytics work together. That’s where the real value is, rather than simply collecting more data.

What challenges will your customers face in the near future?
We’re moving into chiplets, heterogeneous integration, advanced packaging, photonics, and increasingly complex multi-die chip designs. Each introduces additional manufacturing steps, test insertions, and interdependencies. A device may pass through multiple facilities and manufacturing partners before it becomes a finished product. That creates a much larger data management and traceability issue. Engineers need to understand not only whether a particular die or package passed its test limits, but also how the different manufacturing stages contributed to the final device performance. Being able to correlate information across wafer fabrication, assembly, packaging, and final test will become increasingly important.

Another challenge is the sheer volume and complexity of the data. Traditional approaches to data analysis weren’t necessarily designed for the scale and complexity we’re beginning to see. I expect customers will need to find ways to get more value from the data they’re already collecting, while making it easier for teams to identify problems earlier and maintain control as production scales.

How has AI changed your business strategy?
AI has changed how we work and how we approach problems, but it doesn’t change the fundamentals of semiconductor manufacturing. You still need accurate data, process knowledge, and engineering discipline to make sound decisions. We see the greatest opportunity in reducing the time engineers spend preparing, organizing, and correlating data before they can begin analysis. AI-assisted capabilities can help identify patterns, surface relationships across manufacturing data, and make complex information easier to navigate.

Our strategy is to build on the data foundation we’ve developed over the years and incorporate AI where it provides practical value. We see it as a way to extend engineering capabilities, not replace the experience and judgment required to make production decisions.
